stem: A **stakeholder** in a business is best defined as

options.content: any person or group that has an interest in the business
options.rationale: Correct: it covers anyone affected by the business or able to affect it.

options.content: only the people who own the shares in the business concerned
options.rationale: Shareholders are one kind of stakeholder, not the whole definition.

options.content: only the people who are paid a regular wage by the firm
options.rationale: Employees are one stakeholder group; customers and the community are others.

options.content: only the customers who regularly buy goods from the business
options.rationale: Customers are one stakeholder group among many.

explanation: A stakeholder is any individual or group affected by, or able to affect, the business.

stem: Which of these is an **internal** stakeholder of a business?

options.content: A worker employed in the firm's factory
options.rationale: Correct: employees are part of the organisation.

options.content: A bank that has lent money to the firm
options.rationale: Lenders are external stakeholders.

options.content: A supplier who delivers raw materials
options.rationale: Suppliers are external to the firm.

options.content: A pressure group campaigning about pollution
options.rationale: Pressure groups are outside the firm.

explanation: Owners, managers and employees are internal stakeholders; all others are external.

stem: What is the main interest of **lenders** such as banks in a business?

options.content: A share of the profit in the form of dividends
options.rationale: Dividends go to shareholders, not lenders.

options.content: Lower prices for the goods the firm sells
options.rationale: Prices matter to customers, not to lenders.

options.content: A voice in choosing the board of directors
options.rationale: Lenders do not vote for directors; shareholders do.

options.content: Repayment of the loan together with interest
options.rationale: Correct: the bank wants its money back and the agreed interest.

explanation: Lenders seek repayment and interest.

stem: Residents near a fictional quarry in Masvingo complain about dust and noise. Which type of stakeholder are they?

options.content: Internal stakeholders who help to run the quarry
options.rationale: Residents do not work for or own the quarry.

options.content: Owners with a right to a share of the profit
options.rationale: Residents have no ownership of the quarry.

options.content: Suppliers who deliver materials to the quarry
options.rationale: They are not described as supplying anything.

options.content: External stakeholders from the local community
options.rationale: Correct: they are outside the firm and affected by its operation.

explanation: Local residents are external stakeholders affected by the firm's operations.

stem: A fictional firm closes its branch in Mutare to cut costs. Which stakeholder gains the **most clearly** from the decision?

options.content: The workers at the branch, because they lose their jobs
options.rationale: Workers who lose their jobs are harmed by the closure.

options.content: The shareholders, because lower costs may raise their profit
options.rationale: Correct: lower costs help profit and dividends.

options.content: The customers of the branch, because they lose a nearby shop
options.rationale: Customers lose a convenient shop, which is a harm.

options.content: The local community, because spending in the area falls
options.rationale: Lower local spending is a harm to the community.

explanation: Cutting costs helps profit and so benefits shareholders; the other groups lose.
hints: Which group benefits when costs fall?

stem: A fictional bakery is the only buyer of flour from a small mill, and the mill has no other customers. Which statement about the relative power of the stakeholders is most likely correct?

options.content: The mill has more power over the bakery because it makes the flour
options.rationale: The mill cannot easily sell to others, so it depends on the bakery.

options.content: Neither has any power over the other, because both are external stakeholders
options.rationale: Dependence gives power; external stakeholders can be very powerful.

options.content: The bakery has more power over the mill than the mill has over it
options.rationale: Correct: the mill depends entirely on one customer.

options.content: The mill and the bakery have exactly equal power over each other
options.rationale: Equal power is unlikely when one depends wholly on the other.

explanation: The side with the alternatives has the greater power; the mill has none.
hints: Ask which firm could easily find an alternative.

stem: Which situation is the clearest example of a **conflict** between stakeholders' aims?

options.content: Customers and owners both want the firm to remain in business for many years
options.rationale: Both want the same thing, so there is no conflict.

options.content: Shareholders want higher dividends and workers want higher pay from one profit
options.rationale: Correct: both groups want a larger share of the same profit.

options.content: Suppliers and managers both want orders to be delivered to customers on time
options.rationale: Both want smooth deliveries; there is no conflict.

options.content: Lenders and the bank manager both want the loan to be repaid on time
options.rationale: They share the same aim.

explanation: Conflict arises when the aims of two groups cannot both be fully met.
hints: Look for two groups wanting a bigger share of the same thing.

stem: Which is the **most convincing** judgement on whether a firm should put shareholders' interests above all others?

options.content: Yes, because shareholders own the firm and so nobody else really matters at all
options.rationale: Others can affect the firm's survival and profit, so they matter.

options.content: No, because shareholders have no real interest in the firm's profit or dividends
options.rationale: Shareholders are chiefly interested in profit.

options.content: No, because unhappy workers, customers or neighbours can reduce the shareholders' profit
options.rationale: Correct: it links other stakeholders' reactions to the shareholders' own aim.

options.content: Yes, because other groups never react to the firm's decisions in any way
options.rationale: Workers, customers and others do react, as strikes and boycotts show.

explanation: A convincing judgement shows that ignoring other stakeholders can damage the profit that shareholders want.
hints: Choose the answer that gives a reason connected to the firm's results.

stem: Customers, suppliers and the government are external stakeholders.
explanation: True. They are outside the organisation but have an interest in it or can influence it.

stem: A stakeholder with a strong interest in a decision always has the most influence over it.
explanation: False. Influence depends on power, organisation, alternatives and legal rights, not on interest alone; local residents may care a great deal but have little power.
hints: Think about residents who object to a factory but cannot stop it.

stem: Match each stakeholder to its main interest.

right.content: Quality goods at a fair price
Tax revenue and compliance with the law
Dividends and growth in the value of their shares
Pay, job security and safe working conditions

explanation: Each stakeholder group has a distinct main interest.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: Managers are {{blank:a}} to the owners of the business, which means they must explain and justify their {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Accountability means being obliged to explain and justify decisions and results.

stem: State **one** way in which a pressure group might influence a business.
explanation: Pressure groups campaign, protest, call for boycotts and publicise the firm's behaviour.

stem: A fictional company earned a profit of US\$60,000. Its board decides to pay 35% of the profit to shareholders as dividends. How much will shareholders receive in total?
explanation: 35% of 60,000 = 60,000 × 35 ÷ 100 = US\$21,000. The remaining US\$39,000 is left for other uses, which is the wrong answer if you take the balance.
workedSolution: 1. 35% of 60,000 = 60,000 × 35 ÷ 100 = US\$21,000. The remaining US\$39,000 is left for other uses, which is the wrong answer if you take the balance.

stem: A fictional workshop in Bulawayo shares a bonus pool of US\$9,000 equally among its 15 workers. How much does each worker receive?
explanation: Each worker receives 9,000 ÷ 15 = US\$600.
hints: Divide the pool by the number of workers.

stem: After a union negotiation, the yearly wage bill of a fictional firm rises from US\$80,000 to US\$86,400. Calculate the percentage increase to one decimal place.
explanation: The increase is 86,400 − 80,000 = 6,400. 6,400 ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 8.0%. Dividing by the new figure gives 7.4%.
workedSolution: 1. The increase is 86,400 − 80,000 = 6,400. 6,400 ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 8.0%. Dividing by the new figure gives 7.4%.
hints: Percentage change is the increase divided by the original figure.

stem: Distinguish between an internal and an external stakeholder.

points.description: An internal stakeholder is part of the organisation, such as owners, managers and employees
An external stakeholder is outside it, such as customers, suppliers, lenders, government and the community

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Internal stakeholders belong to the organisation, such as owners, managers and workers. External stakeholders are outside it, such as customers, suppliers, banks and the community.

explanation: One mark for each type, with examples.

stem: Rudo owns a fictional chicken farm in Chinhoyi and plans to double output. Explain how this decision could affect **two** stakeholders.

points.description: Workers: more jobs and overtime
Application: more staff are needed to look after the extra birds
Neighbours or the community: more smell, noise and waste
Application: residents may complain or demand action from the council

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Workers may gain more jobs and overtime because more staff are needed for the extra birds. Neighbours may suffer more smell, noise and waste, so they might complain to the council or campaign against the farm.

explanation: Two stakeholders, each with a developed effect.
hints: Choose two groups and say whether each gains or loses.

stem: Analyse why conflict may arise between shareholders and workers after a profitable year.

points.description: Shareholders want a high share of the profit as dividends
Workers want higher pay or a bonus from the same profit
Each pound or dollar paid to one group reduces what is left for the other
Unresolved conflict can lower morale or cause strikes, harming future profit

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Shareholders expect dividends and workers expect higher pay, but both are paid from the same profit, so more for one means less for the other. If workers feel they are treated unfairly, morale falls or they strike, which reduces future profit for everyone.

explanation: The source of conflict and its consequence.
hints: Follow what happens to the same profit when each group asks for more.

stem: Assess whether the community or the bank is the more influential stakeholder when a fictional factory plans to expand.

points.description: The bank can refuse or call in a loan, which stops the expansion
The community can protest, complain to the council and damage the firm's reputation
The bank has legal rights and financial power; the community has fewer formal powers
The community's influence increases if it is organised or supported by the council
Judgement with a reason or condition

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The bank can refuse finance, which would stop the expansion at once, and it has legal rights to repayment. The community has less formal power but can protest and complain to the council, which could delay or stop the plan. On balance the bank is more influential, unless the community is well organised and the council supports it.

explanation: Both groups compared, with a conditional judgement.
hints: Compare power and rights, then state what the judgement depends on.

stem: A fictional business: Zambezi Cement (Victoria Falls) made a profit of US\$90,000. The board proposes to pay 50% as dividends, 20% as a bonus to its 30 workers and keep the rest. The workers' union says the bonus is too small. Residents downstream complain about dust from the plant.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total paid as dividends.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the bonus received by each worker if the bonus is shared equally.
parts.explanation: The bonus pool is 20% of 90,000 = US\$18,000. Each worker receives 18,000 ÷ 30 = US\$600.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The bonus pool is 20% of 90,000 = US\$18,000. Each worker receives 18,000 ÷ 30 = US\$600.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Identify **one** internal and **one** external stakeholder in the case and state an interest of each.

points.description: Internal stakeholder with an interest (workers: bonus; shareholders: dividends)
External stakeholder with an interest (residents: less dust; government: tax)
Both stakeholders correctly classified and their interests linked to the case

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The workers are internal stakeholders and want a larger bonus. The residents are external stakeholders and want less dust from the plant.

parts.explanation: One mark for each stakeholder and interest, one for correct classification.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** way in which the board could reduce the conflict with the union.

points.description: Consult or negotiate with the union about the bonus
Application: raise the bonus by reducing the share kept or dividends slightly

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The board could meet the union and negotiate, perhaps raising the bonus a little by reducing the amount kept in the business.

parts.explanation: A method, applied to the case.

explanation: The shares of the profit are calculated and stakeholder interests and conflict are discussed.
hints: Use percentages of the profit for the first two parts.

stem: A fictional business: Tendai runs Hwange Coal Supplies, which employs 120 workers and sells coal to a power plant that takes 60% of its output. The bank that financed new trucks wants its loan repaid in two years. An environmental group wants the firm to reduce dust and has asked customers to boycott it. The power plant says it will take less coal if prices rise.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Analyse the power of **one** stakeholder over the firm.

points.description: The power plant buys 60% of output
It could reduce orders if prices rise
The firm's income would fall sharply
The firm could find it hard to replace such a large customer

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The power plant buys 60% of the firm's coal, so it controls most of the firm's income. If prices rise it can reduce orders, and the firm might struggle to find another large customer.

parts.explanation: The source of power and its effect.
hints: Choose one group and say what it can do to the firm.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how the aims of the bank and the environmental group may conflict with those of the workers.

points.description: The bank wants quick repayment, which may mean cost cutting
Cost cutting may mean fewer jobs or lower pay
The group wants dust reduced, which costs money
Extra cost may reduce the funds for repayments or wages

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The bank wants repayment within two years, which may require cuts in costs and fewer jobs. The environmental group wants the dust to be reduced, which costs money and may further reduce what is available for wages and repayments.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate which stakeholder Tendai should give priority to.

points.description: The power plant: most important customer and source of income
The bank: legal right to repayment, can threaten the firm
The workers: skilled labour needed but easier to replace than the main customer
The environmental group: can harm reputation but least formal power
Judgement that ranks the groups
A condition or time-frame for the judgement

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The power plant buys 60% of output, so losing it would end the firm's income, which makes it the most important. The bank also has a legal right to repayment and can force action. The workers matter but are easier to replace, and the environmental group has the least formal power, although its boycott could damage the firm's reputation. Tendai should give priority to the power plant and the bank, while taking low-cost steps to reduce the dust so that the group's pressure does not grow, and he should review the position if more customers join the boycott.

parts.explanation: The groups are ranked with reasons and a condition.
hints: Rank the groups by power, then add a condition.

explanation: Power is analysed, conflicts explained and priorities evaluated.
hints: Quote the case, such as 60% of output.
